genxml.title: Cobalt (system ASIC of the SGI Visual Workstation 320 and 540): the CPU block and the interrupt controller, as SGI's Linux platform code names them
genxml.doc: Offsets, bit positions and values come from the Linux Visual Workstation code (kernel 2.2 to 3.14) and are cross-checked against SGI's shipped Windows NT 4.0 HAL (halborg.dll 1.3). Grades: established means the shipped HAL programs the item the same way (or the item is its own table); inferred means only Linux defines it, a software expectation of Linux and not of the shipped system. Where the HAL differs, the item says so. The chip's own specification is not held. Offsets are relative to the base of each block (CPU_PHYS and APIC_PHYS below). Linux reads and writes every register as a 32-bit word. Reset values are unknown throughout. Only what the kernel touches is here; the memory controller and graphics engine registers are not.

struct.name: APIC_LO
struct.doc: Interrupt redirection entry, low word, one per interrupt line (thirty lines, 0 to 29). The kernel writes the level bit and an interrupt vector to unmask a line and only the mask bit to mask it, reading the register back after masking. The vector it writes is the kernel's irq number plus 0x20, so it is not the line number.

struct.name: APIC_HI
struct.doc: Interrupt redirection entry, high word. The kernel writes zero beside every low word it sets and never reads it. By the standard I/O APIC layout it would hold the destination processor; that is inferred from the layout of the low word and the register spacing, and no code reads it back.

struct.name: APIC_ID
struct.doc: Controller identification and enable. The kernel reads it, sets the enable bit with a read-modify-write that it says must not change the identification, and prints the result. Where the identification field sits is not known.

struct.name: CPU_REV
struct.doc: Cobalt revision. The kernel prints it at start-up and, in the 2.4 interrupt path, reads it after a driver has acknowledged its device as a way to make sure the driver's write has reached the device before the end-of-interrupt. The field layout is not known.

struct.name: CPU_CTRL
struct.doc: Timer and memory control. Linux sets timer_run and clears timer_mask, each by a read-modify-write, after loading the count, and touches no other bit. The NT HAL (halborg.dll 1.3: the Cobalt control set-up in HalInitSystem and HalpEccControl) also clears ecc_enable at start-up, sets timer_mask, ORs in page_close from its PAGEOPENPOLICY boot option, and sets ecc_enable together with bit 0 of the memory block when it enables ECC.

struct.name: CPU_STAT
struct.doc: Timer status. The 2.2 and 2.4 timer handlers clear the pending bit by reading the register and writing it back with that bit cleared. The 2.5 and later code never writes it, so whether a level timer interrupt needs this clear to deassert is open.

struct.name: CPU_TIMEVAL
struct.doc: Timer count. The kernel writes the Cobalt core rate divided by the tick rate (a 100 MHz core rate) before starting the timer and calls it a countdown value. That it reloads itself each period is inferred from the kernel using it as the periodic tick and writing it once.
